Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette: Ahmad is a 37-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a firefighter and lives with his wife in a suburban neighborhood. Ahmad’s life changed dramatically after he became the target of an intense stalking incident that left him feeling unsafe and overwhelmed. The traumatic event occurred about six months ago, when a former colleague began to stalk Ahmad relentlessly, following him to work and even showing up at his home unannounced. Since then, Ahmad has been acutely aware of specific triggers that remind him of the incident. For example, whenever he rides his bicycle or visits locations where he had previously encountered his stalker, he feels an intense sense of vulnerability. These spatial triggers often lead to vivid and overwhelming memories of being followed and tracked. One day while riding his bike home from work, Ahmad suddenly found himself in a place where the stalker had confronted him before. The memory came back unbidden, leaving him feeling so overwhelmed that he had to stop cycling and sit by the roadside until the intensity passed. These triggers have also reinforced Ahmad’s negative appraisals about himself and his situation. He believes he has permanently changed for the worse since the stalking began. This belief in his permanent damage often manifests as fear that his reactions mean he is going crazy, and it makes him feel weak and unable to cope with everyday life. For instance, he has started scanning every room he enters for exits and watching people closely for any signs of potential harm. These actions are driven by his deep-seated belief that he must be vigilant at all times. The memory itself adds another layer of distress. Ahmad’s inability to find words to describe what happened leaves him feeling isolated and misunderstood. When the memories return, they often do so without warning, triggered by something in his surroundings. Once triggered, the memories overwhelm him with a flood of emotions that he struggles to articulate or process. These overwhelming memories not only reinforce his negative appraisals but also increase his sense of threat. For example, whenever Ahmad finds himself in locations where he has been followed before, the memories flood back, heightening his fear and making him feel even more threatened by unexpected sounds or sudden movements from others around him. This heightened sense of threat further solidifies his belief that he is weak and unable to handle these situations. Over time, Ahmad’s occupational life as a firefighter has been impacted significantly. He struggles to perform his duties with the same confidence and effectiveness due to his constant vigilance and fear of being followed or tracked in public spaces. His performance at work has declined, leading to concerns from his colleagues and supervisors about his ability to handle emergencies effectively. Ahmad’s marriage has also suffered as a result of these symptoms. He often withdraws from social activities with his wife, fearing that he might be triggered by something she says or does. This has led to increased tension in their relationship and left Ahmad feeling more isolated than ever before. Despite the intensity of his symptoms, it was only after a particularly distressing incident at work that Ahmad decided to seek help. He had been assigned to a call near one of the locations where he had encountered his stalker, and the memories overwhelmed him so much that he became unable to focus on his tasks. This realization that his reactions were not just affecting his personal life but also endangering his professional responsibilities finally pushed him to reach out for assistance. Ahmad is most afraid that these feelings of weakness and fear will continue indefinitely and prevent him from living a normal life. At the same time, he hopes that therapy can help him regain control over his thoughts and actions, allowing him to return to work and strengthen his relationship with his wife without the constant dread of being followed or attacked.
